summary.text: For odd \(k>61\), write \(k=2n+1\) and swap the two primes in the assumed representation to obtain \(k=q+2p\); the remaining odd cases \(5<k\le 61\) are handled by a finite computation. For twin primes, if the admissible primes \(p\) were bounded by \(N\), applying the hypothesis to half of \((2N+2)!\) would give a prime \(q=(2N+2)!-(2p-1)\), although \(2p-1>1\) is a proper divisor of \(q\); hence there are infinitely many such \(p\), and the injective map \(p\mapsto\operatorname{prime}(p+2)\) yields infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

full_proof.text:
Let \(P_m\) denote the \(m\)-th prime in the usual one-indexed ordering, so \(P_1=2,P_2=3,\ldots\). Thus the expression \(\operatorname{prime}(p+2)\) in the conjecture is \(P_{p+2}\).

Assume part (ii) of the A236566 conjecture. In explicit terms, our hypothesis is:

\[
\tag{H}
\text{for every }n>30\text{ there are primes }p,q\text{ such that }
P_{p+2}+2\text{ is prime and }2n+1=2p+q.
\]

We prove separately that (H) implies the twin prime conjecture and Lemoine's conjecture.

## 1. An infinite auxiliary set

Define
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }P_{p+2}+2\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
We first prove that \(S\) is infinite.

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(S\) is finite. It then has an upper bound. Choose an integer \(N\ge 30\) which is also an upper bound for \(S\); that is,
\[
p\le N\qquad\text{for every }p\in S.
\]
For example, one may take the maximum of \(30\) and the largest element of \(S\), with the empty case handled by simply using \(30\).

Set
\[
M=(2N+2)!,\qquad n=\frac M2.
\]
Because \(2\le 2N+2\), the integer \(2\) divides \(M\), so \(M=2n\). Also
\[
M=(2N+2)!\ge 2N+2\ge 62.
\]
It follows from \(M=2n\) that \(n\ge31\), hence \(n>30\). We may therefore apply (H) to this \(n\). We obtain primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
P_{p+2}+2\text{ is prime},
\qquad M+1=2n+1=2p+q.
\]
The two primality conditions on \(p\) show that \(p\in S\), and hence \(p\le N\).

Consider
\[
d=2p-1.
\]
Every prime is at least \(2\), so \(d\ge3\), in particular \(d>0\). Moreover, from \(p\le N\),
\[
d=2p-1\le 2N-1<2N+2.
\]
Thus \(d\) is one of the positive integers not exceeding \(2N+2\), and consequently
\[
d\mid (2N+2)!=M.
\]
On the other hand, rearranging \(M+1=2p+q\) gives
\[
q=M-(2p-1)=M-d.
\]
Since \(d\mid M\), this identity shows that \(d\mid q\).

We next check that this divisor is proper. Using the factorial recurrence and \(N\ge30\),
\[
M=(2N+2)(2N+1)!.
\]
Here \((2N+1)!\ge2\), and therefore
\[
M\ge 2(2N+2)=4N+4>4N.
\]
Since \(p\le N\), we have
\[
2d=4p-2\le4N-2<4N<M.
\]
Thus \(M-d>d\), or equivalently
\[
q>d.
\]
We have now found a divisor \(d\) of the prime \(q\) satisfying
\[
1<d<q.
\]
That is impossible, since the only positive divisors of a prime are \(1\) and the prime itself. This contradiction proves that \(S\) is infinite.

## 2. The twin prime conjecture

For each \(p\in S\), put
\[
f(p)=P_{p+2}.
\]
By definition, \(f(p)\) is prime, and because \(p\in S\), the number
\[
f(p)+2=P_{p+2}+2
\]
is also prime. Hence every member of \(f(S)\) is the smaller member of a twin-prime pair.

The map \(f\) is injective: the sequence of primes \(P_1,P_2,\ldots\) is strictly increasing, so
\[
P_{a+2}=P_{b+2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a+2=b+2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=b.
\]
As \(S\) is infinite, its injective image \(f(S)\) is infinite. Therefore there are infinitely many primes \(r\) for which \(r+2\) is prime. This is exactly the twin prime conjecture.

## 3. Lemoine's conjecture

We must prove that every odd integer \(k>5\) can be written
\[
k=r+2s
\]
with both \(r\) and \(s\) prime.

First suppose that \(k>61\). Since \(k\) is odd, there is an integer
\[
n=\frac{k-1}{2}
\]
for which \(k=2n+1\). The least odd integer greater than \(61\) is \(63\), so \(n\ge31\), and hence \(n>30\). Applying (H), choose primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
2n+1=2p+q.
\]
(The additional condition that \(P_{p+2}+2\) is prime is not needed in this part of the argument.) Since \(k=2n+1\), we have
\[
k=q+2p.
\]
Thus Lemoine's representation is obtained by taking \(r=q\) and \(s=p\), both of which are prime.

It remains only to handle the odd integers \(k\) with \(5<k\le61\). The following table supplies a representation \(k=r+2s\) in every case:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
k&(r,s)&k&(r,s)&k&(r,s)\\ \hline
 7&(3,2)& 9&(3,3)&11&(5,3)\\
13&(3,5)&15&(5,5)&17&(3,7)\\
19&(5,7)&21&(7,7)&23&(13,5)\\
25&(3,11)&27&(5,11)&29&(3,13)\\
31&(5,13)&33&(7,13)&35&(13,11)\\
37&(3,17)&39&(5,17)&41&(3,19)\\
43&(5,19)&45&(7,19)&47&(13,17)\\
49&(3,23)&51&(5,23)&53&(7,23)\\
55&(17,19)&57&(11,23)&59&(13,23)\\
61&(3,29)&&&
\end{array}
\]

In each displayed pair, both entries are prime, and direct substitution gives \(k=r+2s\). These are all the odd integers strictly between \(5\) and \(62\), so the finite range is complete.

Consequently every odd \(k>5\) is a prime plus twice a prime, proving Lemoine's conjecture. Together with Section 2, this shows that part (ii) of the A236566 conjecture implies both Lemoine's conjecture and the twin prime conjecture.
